title-group.article-title: On Computing Degree-Based Topological Invariants for Special Graphs

abstract.p: Topological indices represent an important class of mathematical tools for studying the structural properties of graphs and have various applications in mathematical chemistry, especially in analyzing the structural properties of molecules and quantitative structure-activity relationship. Among degree-based topological indices based on degree, the Sombor indices are useful in determining the structural properties of graphs based on the degrees of adjacent vertices. In this paper, the Sombor index (\(SO\)), the reduced Sombor index (\(SO_{\mathrm{red}}\)), and the average Sombor index (\(SO_{\mathrm{avg}}\)) of several special graph classes were studied. These include the Web graphs, Windmill graphs, Dutch Windmill graphs, double graphs of Dutch Windmill graphs, and strong double graphs of Dutch Windmill graphs. Degree partitions of these special graph classes were calculated and the expressions of three Sombor indices were determined using structural parameters. These expressions were then analyzed numerically and graphically in order to investigate the behavior of the Sombor type indices as the graph parameters increased. It was found numerically that all three Sombor indices exhibited an increasing trend over the range of parameters considered and consistently satisfied the order \(SO(G) > SO_{\mathrm{red}}(G) > SO_{\mathrm{avg}}(G)\). Furthermore, the double and strong double graphs had considerably higher Sombor indices when compared to their corresponding Dutch Windmill graphs. This shows how adding more connections to a graph increases the degree-based Sombor descriptors. From the above results, one can conclude that the Sombor type indices successfully reflect the variation in the degree distribution and connectivity arising from different graph constructions.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The origin of graph theory was traditionally dated back to year 1736, when Euler solved the famous Königsberg bridges problem [1]. Graph theory is one of the few mathematical areas of study that have an exact date of emergence. Kirchhoff's research into electrical networks directed his progress of basic theory as well as ideas about trees in graphs, while Cayley considered trees from the calculation of isomers as living chemicals. Another form of graph paradox was suggested by Hamilton. Graph theory, a branch of mathematics relating to network points connected by lines, has its origin in recreational mathematical problems but has grown into the core of mathematical research through chemistry, occupational research, social science, and computer science. A graph \(G\) consists of a set of nodes \(V=\{u_1,u_2,u_3,\ldots\}\) and the other set \(E=\{e_{i_1},e_{i_2},e_{i_3},\ldots\}\) whose elements are called arcs. If \(e_i=u_1 u_2\) is an arc of graph \(G\), then the nodes \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) are adjacent in \(G\). When any two nodes are connected by more than one arc, the graph is called a multigraph. A numerical value associated with each node is its degree.

The topological descriptor is the nominal value associated with the graph and must be a structural variable. Several topological descriptors have been described and most of them have found properties as a modeling of chemicals, drugs, and other molecular structures. The Wiener index [2], [3], [4] is the first topological descriptor used in chemistry. Topological descriptors are statistical measures of a graph of cells that remain constant under the graph isomorphism. Started their journey in 1947, a wide variety of topological descriptors have been created and much work has been done on graphs of various cells and networks. Likewise, Harold Wiener introduced and developed this intriguing guide to determine the physical characteristics of alkane species known as paraffin in 1947. Topological descriptors are of incompatible types as degree-based topological descriptors, distance-based topological descriptors, and spectrum-based [5], [6] topological descriptors.

To adopt an applied mathematical approach, graphs like web, windmill, and Dutch windmill graphs are very useful and idealized models of networks having a central or a well-connected center along with peripheral or repeating components. These graphs can be used to model connectivity patterns in case of molecular and chemical networks, communication or transport networks, and many other types of complex network models that include interaction between a few well-connected units and many other less connected units. In the case of the chemical graph model, such a type of family of graphs is quite suitable to depict simple models of molecular frameworks involving branchings and repeating parts of molecules along with the concept of hubs. The use of double and strong double construction allows us to investigate the effect of increasing connectivity and coupling between the parts of graphs [7], [8]. In this paper, the Sombor indices calculated for these graph models considered the degree of vertices as a measure of structural irregularity, and thus the comparison of these indices could be helpful in distinguishing the features of these families of graphs.

sec.title: 3. Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we investigated the Sombor index (\(SO\)), reduced Sombor index (\(SO_{\mathrm{red}}\)), and average Sombor index (\(SO_{\mathrm{avg}}\)) for several special graph families, including web graphs, windmill graphs, Dutch windmill graphs, and the double and strong double graphs of Dutch windmill graphs. The key mathematical observation is that the values of these degree-based indices are strongly influenced by the degree distribution of the underlying graph. Since the Sombor type indices are defined in terms of the degrees of adjacent vertices, changes in vertex degrees and in the connectivity between vertices directly affect their numerical values.
For all the considered graph families and parameter ranges, the numerical results consistently show the ordering

Furthermore, the values of all three indices increased as the parameters of the corresponding graph families enlarged, hence reflecting the effect of the growing graph structure and its degree distribution. The double graph construction introduces additional connections between the two copies of the Dutch windmill graph and consequently produces substantially larger values of the Sombor indices. The strong double construction provides an even stronger coupling between the two copies through the adjacency relations, resulting in a further increase in the index values. Thus, the numerical comparisons demonstrate that increasing connectivity through double and strong double graph operations has a significant effect on degree-based Sombor indices.

Overall, the obtained formulas and numerical comparisons indicated that the Sombor indices provided a useful means of distinguishing the structural changes caused by different graph constructions. In particular, the changes in degree distribution and connectivity induced by the double and strong double operations are explicitly mirrored in the magnitudes and growth patterns of \(SO\), \(SO_{\mathrm{red}}\), and \(SO_{\mathrm{avg}}\).
